claim: Over defined operating conditions and with sufficient data, non-trivial error models of learned discrete-time robotic dynamical systems can be determined such that the error model always over estimates the true error up to a statistical confidence.
subclaims: Under what operating conditions can non-trivial error models be determined?
Is sufficient data required to determine non-trivial error models?
What type of systems are the error models for?
Do the error models always overestimate the true error?
Is the overestimation of true error bounded by a statistical confidence?
baseline_experiments: To address subclaim 1, 'Under what operating conditions can non-trivial error models be determined?', and subclaim 3, 'What type of systems are the error models for?', use public robotic transition datasets such as D4RL/Minari MuJoCo locomotion tasks on HuggingFace or Gymnasium/Minari, e.g. Hopper, Walker2d, HalfCheetah, and Ant. Train learned discrete-time dynamics models that predict next state from current state and action. Define operating conditions by restricting evaluation to regions of state-action space with measurable dataset support, for example by density level sets, k-nearest-neighbor distance thresholds, policy/task identity, velocity ranges, or action magnitude ranges. For each operating region, train a non-trivial error model, such as an ensemble-uncertainty model or residual quantile regressor with conformal calibration, that predicts an upper bound on one-step or multi-step prediction error. Compare the learned local bound against a trivial global constant bound, such as the 95th or 99th percentile residual over all calibration data. If learned bounds maintain target coverage while being substantially tighter than the global bound only in high-support regions, this would suggest that non-trivial error models are feasible only under well-covered operating conditions. If bounds remain tight and calibrated across multiple robot morphologies and broad support regions, this supports the claim for learned discrete-time robotic dynamical systems more generally. If bounds fail or become vacuous outside the support of the training data, this weakens any broad interpretation of the claim. This experiment could be made less necessary if the claim supplied precise operating-condition definitions and prior empirical evidence showing calibrated non-trivial bounds across several public robotic systems.

To address subclaim 2, 'Is sufficient data required to determine non-trivial error models?', perform a learning-curve study on the same public D4RL/Minari datasets. Fix an operating condition identified in Experiment 1, then train the learned dynamics model and error model using increasing fractions of the available trajectories, for example 1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100%, with separate train, calibration, and test splits. For each data size, measure empirical coverage of the predicted error upper bound, average bound width, violation rate, and improvement over a trivial global bound. Repeat over random seeds and report confidence intervals. If small datasets produce either undercoverage or very wide/vacuous bounds while larger datasets yield calibrated and tighter bounds, this supports the subclaim that sufficient data is required. If useful calibrated bounds appear with very little data, the sufficiency requirement may be weaker than stated. If no amount of available data yields non-trivial calibrated bounds, the claim is not supported for that system or operating condition. This experiment could be made unnecessary or reduced in scope if theoretical sample-complexity results or prior learning-curve evidence were provided for the specific dynamics and error-model class.

To address subclaim 4, 'Do the error models always overestimate the true error?', and subclaim 5, 'Is the overestimation of true error bounded by a statistical confidence?', evaluate the calibrated error models from Experiments 1 and 2 on held-out trajectories using split conformal prediction or another finite-sample-valid calibration method. For each held-out transition or rollout, compute whether the predicted upper error bound is at least the realized model error, then test whether the empirical violation rate is consistent with the nominal confidence level, such as 90%, 95%, or 99%, using binomial confidence intervals. Run both in-distribution tests and deliberate distribution-shift tests, such as evaluating a Hopper model trained on medium-expert data against random or medium-replay data, to see whether the guarantee holds only under exchangeability or defined operating conditions. If the in-distribution empirical violation rate is at or below the target level and bounds are non-vacuous, this supports the statistical-confidence part of the claim, though not literal deterministic 'always' coverage. If violations exceed the nominal level, especially under nominal operating conditions, the claim is weakened. If failures occur primarily under distribution shift, the conclusion is that the claim must explicitly restrict operating conditions and assumptions such as exchangeability. This experiment could be made unnecessary if a formal conformal or PAC-style proof were provided together with evidence that the dataset and deployment setting satisfy the proof assumptions.
method_experiments: To address subclaim 4 and subclaim 5, run a held-out coverage test of learned error upper bounds for discrete-time robot dynamics. Use public trajectory datasets such as HuggingFace `edbeeching/decision_transformer_gym_replay` / D4RL-style Hopper, Walker2d, and HalfCheetah data, where each transition is `(state_t, action_t, state_{t+1})`. Train a nominal learned dynamics model, e.g. an MLP or ensemble predicting `state_{t+1}-state_t`, on a training split. Then train an error model predicting an upper bound on the one-step prediction error norm, using a separate calibration split with conformal prediction, quantile regression, or GP/ensemble uncertainty scaling. Evaluate on independent test trajectories whether the empirical violation rate `Pr(true error > predicted bound)` is no larger than the target level alpha, and use an exact binomial or Clopper-Pearson interval to decide whether the claimed confidence level is met. Also compare against a trivial constant bound equal to a high global quantile or maximum calibration error; call the error model non-trivial only if it is significantly tighter while maintaining coverage. If the learned bound covers at least `1-alpha` of test errors with a lower confidence bound above the target and is tighter than the trivial baseline, this supports the overestimation-with-confidence part of the claim under those conditions. If coverage fails, the claim is not feasible without stronger assumptions or more conservative bounds. This experiment could be made unnecessary if there were already independent benchmark results showing statistically valid calibrated coverage for non-trivial learned dynamics error bounds on the same public robotic systems.

To address subclaim 2, perform a sample-complexity ablation to test whether sufficient data is required to obtain non-trivial valid error models. On the same public D4RL/HuggingFace robot transition datasets, repeat the first experiment while varying the number of training and calibration transitions, for example 1k, 5k, 10k, 50k, and 100k transitions, with multiple random trajectory-level splits. For each data size, measure: one-step dynamics prediction error, empirical coverage of the error bound, statistical confidence interval for the violation rate, average bound width, and improvement over the trivial constant bound. Possible conclusions are: if small datasets either under-cover or require nearly trivial wide bounds, while larger datasets achieve calibrated and tighter bounds, this supports the subclaim that sufficient data is required; if even small datasets yield valid non-trivial bounds, the data requirement is weaker than claimed; if no data size achieves non-trivial calibrated bounds, the feasibility of the main claim is doubtful for the chosen systems or model class. This experiment could be made unnecessary if prior evidence provided explicit learning curves showing the amount of data needed for valid calibrated error bounds on learned robotic dynamics.

To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 3, map the operating conditions and system types for which non-trivial error models can be determined. Use several public discrete-time robotic datasets with different dynamics, such as Hopper/Walker2d/HalfCheetah locomotion from D4RL-style HuggingFace datasets and a manipulation dataset from HuggingFace LeRobot, e.g. PushT or a real robot manipulation trajectory dataset if state-action-next-state information is available. Define operating conditions by support density and ranges of state variables, action magnitudes, velocities, contact modes, and trajectory source policy. Train the nominal dynamics and calibrated error model using data from selected operating regions, then test both in-distribution regions and deliberately held-out or low-density regions. Estimate coverage and bound tightness per region. If calibrated non-trivial bounds hold only in high-density, in-distribution regions but fail or become trivial in extrapolation regions, this identifies the operating conditions under which the claim is feasible. If bounds remain valid and tight across systems and operating regimes, the claim is more broadly supported. If results vary strongly by robot class, the claim should be restricted to those learned discrete-time robotic dynamical systems whose data distribution and dynamics regularity permit calibration. This experiment could be made unnecessary if existing evidence already specified validated operating envelopes, including state/action ranges and distribution-shift limits, for non-trivial learned dynamics error models.
